newsitem.title: UK: Norway politics to hamper bonds, focus on budget.
newsitem.headline: Norway politics to hamper bonds, focus on budget.

text.p: A resignation by Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland on Wednesday caught markets on the hop and presented problems for Norwegian bonds as it raised questions about the country's budget, analysts said.

The resignation comes in the middle of budget deliberations and the named successor -- ruling Labour Party chairman Thorbjoern Jagland -- is considered more left-leaning than Bruntland, they told Reuters Financial Television.
"The exact timing is a bit puzzling," said Georg Andersen, chief economist at FIBA Nordic Securities in Oslo.

He said that a time when markets were "obsessed by the effects from a budget on an overheated economy", and with the central bank unlikely to raise interest rates to combat this, markets would be more comfortable with a less left-wing leader.
"Until this doubt has been erased it could leave a situation where Norwegian bonds will have problems in following any further convergence," Andersen said.

Norwegian government bonds at 1017 GMT yielded 82 basis points over benchmark Bunds. That spread is narrower than 84 late in Europe on Tuesday but is wider than below 70 basis points earlier in the month.
"In terms of the bond markets, it has been unable to sustain spread narrowing below 75 basis points versus Bunds recently," said Ian Gunner, international economist at Chase in London.
"This will continue to be the case until the government has made it clear what sort of compromises it's going to put forward to enable the budget to be passed," he said.

Kjetil Groenskag, head of Norwegian research at Alfred Berg in London, also saw short term uncertainty hampering the markets, at least until Jagland had been appointed and then the 1997 budget was approved.

But he added, "Jagland has informally been a kind of prime minister trainee for the past couple of years." As such he has been learning to "polish" his leftist stances and make them more palatable for the markets.
The market, however, will remain fixated by the budget situation, analysts said, although they doubted it would result in tighter credit policy.
"Our own feeling here is that they could give up two to four billion kroner worth of spending (cuts)," Gunner said.
"Okay, they would risk the wrath of the central bank to some degree, but I don't think the central bank is about to turn around and raise interest rates because of that."
